title: The mind like the wind
hookLine: Arjuna says the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; the breath is where you can reach it
carry: arjuna's wind: the mind follows the breath

cards: A hard email, a slammed door, a long line at the pharmacy. Heart pounding, jaw tight, thoughts spinning, and somebody says: just breathe. It's annoying advice, mostly because nobody says why it would help.

The tradition has an answer, and it starts with a complaint. On the battlefield, Krishna has just described a yogi sitting perfectly still, steady as a lamp out of the wind. And Arjuna pushes back: I can't do that.

teach.h: AS HARD TO HOLD AS THE WIND.
teach.b: Arjuna doesn't hold back. The mind is restless, Krishna, he says. Stubborn, strong, it shakes me.
Trying to hold it is like trying to hold the wind. And Krishna doesn't argue. Yes, he says, the mind is restless and hard to hold.
But it can be held, by practice and by letting go. Abhyasa and vairagya: practice, again and again, and loosening your grip on what pulls you away.
That's in the Bhagavad Gita, and Hindu teachers have leaned on it ever since. Here's where the breath comes in. Arjuna compared the mind to wind.

The old yoga manuals take that seriously: breath and mind move together. When the breath is jumpy, the mind is jumpy; when the breath grows slow and steady, the mind follows. You can't grab the wind of your thoughts.
But you can reach the wind in your lungs. So pranayama, breath practice, is a doorway to the mind. Today, a first, gentle change.
Breathe in through the nose for a count of four. Breathe out, through the nose if you can, for a count of six. No holding, no forcing.
Many teachers call the out-breath the settling half, and you can feel why: your heart speeds up a little as you breathe in, and slows a little as you breathe out.
If six strains, use three in and five out; if you get dizzy, stop and breathe normally. The count isn't a test. And when your mind blows away mid-count, that's Arjuna's wind.

how: Many Hindu teachers begin pranayama with slow, even breathing through the nose, the exhale longer than the inhale, sometimes silently repeating a name of God, teaching that a steadier breath brings a steadier mind.

o: a deep breath that fills the lungs
the half of the breath you lengthen
the first breath you take each morning

games.q: what's inside the practice — tap the pairs.
p: said the mind is like the wind
letting go of what pulls you away
the out-breath is the long one

s: Krishna tells Arjuna the mind is easy to control
he agrees it's restless and hard to hold, but says practice and letting go can hold it.
the yoga tradition teaches that breath and mind move together
a jumpy breath, a jumpy mind; slow the breath, and the mind follows.
you should hold your breath at the top of the count
no holding today. just slow, even, and a longer out.

games.q: you're counting four in, six out, and your mind blows off to tomorrow's test. what would Krishna tell Arjuna?
o: you've failed. the mind can't be held.
come back to the count: that's abhyasa, practice.
breathe harder and force the mind still.
games.why: the mind wanders like the wind. coming back, again and again, is the practice Krishna names: abhyasa. and the breath is the handle.

practice: Sit tall and soft, take one ordinary breath to arrive, then breathe in through the nose for four and out slowly for six, counting quietly at whatever speed feels natural. No holding at the top or the bottom.
If you pray, let each out-breath carry a name of God, like Ram, or the sound Om. When the mind drifts, that's the wind; come back. If it strains, shorten both numbers.

wordCard.voice: Out-breath, the half of the breath you lengthen: four counts in, six counts out, the first way this practice steadies the wind of the mind.

orig.note: Sanskrit: practice, doing it again and again; Krishna's answer to the restless mind.

carryVoice: Your line: arjuna's wind: the mind follows the breath. Four in, six out, whenever the wind picks up. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 6.19 (the lamp in a windless place) and 6.33–6.35 (Arjuna: the mind as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna: by practice and dispassion it is held)
Hatha Yoga Pradipika 2.2 (when the breath moves, the mind moves; when the breath is still, the mind is still)
